title: Session 2 — Participant 4 User + Claude Behavior Graphs
goal: Organize an academic paper about race volunteer motivation, including framing literature for study purpose and initial variable analysis.

Step 1.step_name: Analyze collected articles for research question support and framing
Step 1.step_action: Extract content from collected articles that support/frame research question rough drafts

nodes.label: Prompt Claude to frame research questions from the collected volunteer-motivation articles
nodes.detail: Opens a new Claude chat next to the workflow-planning document and asks it to use attached articles to frame research questions about volunteer motivations and race experiences, then browses a local research folder to select the source PDFs before submitting.

nodes.label: Return an initial literature-grounded set of candidate research questions
nodes.detail: After the attached articles quickly hit the chat's 100-image/PDF-page limit, Claude organizes four research-question directions -- motivation structure, motivation and sense of community, motives vs. retention (the 'Hoye gap'), and role of event management/experience -- citing specific existing studies (Hoye, Yildiz, Lammers 1991).

nodes.label: Review Claude's candidate research questions
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's literature-grounded research-question directions.

nodes.label: Narrow the focus to volunteering as a substitute for racing
nodes.detail: The participant tells Claude that what they are looking for is people using race volunteering as a substitute for being able to run the races.

nodes.label: Reframe the research around volunteering as a substitute for racing
nodes.detail: Claude reframes the study around volunteering as a proxy or substitute for participation (injured runners, lottery misses, aging-out runners), with sections such as 'Substitution as a distinct motive' and 'Identity and vicarious participation'.

nodes.label: Ask for the best way to synthesize the collected articles
nodes.detail: The participant reads the substitution framework and asks what the best way is to synthesize the articles they have collected to find this theme and support a research question.

nodes.label: Propose a practical workflow for synthesizing the collected articles
nodes.detail: Recommends building a citation matrix rather than notes; separating direct evidence from adjacent/theoretical scaffolding; mining near-miss scale items for hidden logic; organizing the write-up by claim/argument rather than by article; and writing the synthesis as a funnel from broad to specific. Offers to build an actual synthesis-matrix template or draft literature-review paragraphs.

nodes.label: Agree to the matrix approach and ask how Claude can help with 15 articles
nodes.detail: The participant agrees to the matrix method ('Ok, let's do that') and says they have about 15 articles to cull for the theme, asking how Claude can help.

nodes.label: Design an upload-and-extraction workflow and build the synthesis matrix workbook
nodes.detail: Proposes a 3-step process (user uploads the 15 PDFs, Claude extracts each into a structured matrix, then they cull/organize by relevance tier), then actually builds a two-sheet 'Article synthesis matrix' XLSX workbook (Article Matrix + Claim Map tabs) pre-filled with the two articles already shared (Hoye et al.; Yildiz 2015).

nodes.label: Try to attach the articles and hit the attachment limit
nodes.detail: While Claude builds the workbook, the participant tries to attach the articles and finds that only two PDFs can be attached at a time.

nodes.label: Tell Claude it won't allow more than two PDFs at once
nodes.detail: The participant tells Claude it won't let them attach more than two PDFs at one time.

nodes.label: Review Claude's workbook and plan for organizing the articles
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's description of the two-sheet synthesis workbook and the extraction plan.

nodes.label: Accommodate the attachment limit by proposing batched uploads
nodes.detail: Suggests sending the remaining articles in batches of 2 (or one at a time) and processing each batch into the matrix as it arrives.

nodes.label: Struggle with the upload limit and ask for another way
nodes.detail: The participant keeps trying to upload in batches, then tells Claude they can't add any more articles and asks if there is another way to do this.

nodes.label: Diagnose the attachment issue and propose workaround options
nodes.detail: Frames it as an interface hiccup rather than a hard limit and lists five alternatives: paste article text directly, upload fewer files at once, supply citations for Claude to web-search, have the participant fill in the matrix from the articles, or share links instead of files.

nodes.label: Decide to abandon the article matrix because it would take too much time
nodes.detail: Decides continuing to fight the attachment limits 'will take way too much time and work,' says they'll find a different way to organize the literature review later, and redirects Claude to look at the study's existing instrument instead.

user_response.label: reject
user_response.reasoning: give up the article matrix workflow

Step 2.step_name: Look at quantitative instrument and decide how to organize findings around research questions
Step 2.step_action: input instrument into Claude and ask for preliminary results outline

nodes.label: Turn Claude's attention to the study's existing instrument
nodes.detail: The participant tells Claude to move on from the literature matrix and look at the instrument for this study.

nodes.label: Propose a hybrid instrument design blending existing scales with new substitution items
nodes.detail: Recommends adapting validated SEVMS/PSCS items plus a new 'Substitution Motivation Scale,' outlining five proposed sections: screening/demographics, the new substitution scale, adapted SEVMS items, sense of community/identity, and retention/future-intention items.

nodes.label: Clarify that the instrument already exists, but get interrupted by Claude
nodes.detail: Interrupts the instrument-design proposal to say the instrument is already designed, and asks Claude to help organize the findings output instead.

user_response.label: reject
user_response.reasoning: reject claude's proposal to design a new instrument

nodes.label: Ask how the instrument should be provided and where the participant is in the process
nodes.detail: Claude says a couple of quick things determine how the results output gets set up, and asks how the instrument will be provided and where the participant is in the research process.

nodes.label: Offer to share the instrument via Qualtrics link or Word document
nodes.detail: Asks whether Claude would rather receive the instrument as a Qualtrics link or a downloaded Word version.

nodes.label: Tell user it is safer to upload Word doc rather than Qualtrics survey
nodes.detail: Claude recommends uploading the Word version, since Qualtrics survey links usually require a login to view.

nodes.label: Upload the exported instrument document
nodes.detail: Uploads 'Instrument Exported.docx,' the Qualtrics-exported version of the survey instrument.

nodes.label: Extract and analyze the uploaded instrument's structure into its component scales
nodes.detail: After an initial extraction hiccup (the raw file view didn't return readable text, so Claude pulls the table content directly), organizes the instrument into four item tables -- a 5-item substitution/continued-involvement scale, a 13-item broader motivation set, a 10-item incentive/passion set, and a 3-item future-intention set -- plus two open items, noting the substitution construct is corroborated by an item embedded elsewhere.

nodes.label: Don't understand Claude's UI and ask what one thing Claude needs before building the result output structure
nodes.detail: The participant does not understand the quick-answer buttons Claude sent and asks 'What's that?'

nodes.label: Misunderstand user's question and instead explain the quick-answer buttons feature, and then re-ask in plain text whether response data has already been collected
nodes.detail: Explains they're just tappable shortcuts and, since they may not be rendering, re-asks in plain text whether response data has already been collected.

nodes.label: Point out that Claude's question got cut off
nodes.detail: Notes that Claude said it needed to know one thing and then seemingly got stuck without asking it.

nodes.label: Restate the data-collection question in plain text
nodes.detail: Confirms it will use plain text this time and asks directly whether survey response data has already been collected or the instrument is still blank.

nodes.label: Confirm real survey data already exists and ask what research questions it can address
nodes.detail: Confirms data collection is already complete and asks for research-question ideas the existing dataset can support, before analyzing anything.

nodes.label: Propose an initial slate of research questions mapped directly onto the instrument's variables
nodes.detail: Returns descriptive, comparative (using the runner-status/participation-history items as a real comparison-group design), predictive/relational, and convergent-validity/mixed-methods question categories tied to specific instrument items.

nodes.label: Review Claude's answer and question whether 'substitution motivation' is an established term in the volunteering literature as the participant is feeling suspicious if Claude coins the term itself
nodes.detail: Pauses the research-question drafting to ask whether there's actual literature on 'substitution motivation' in volunteering.

nodes.label: Research and ground the substitution-motivation concept in leisure-substitutability theory
nodes.detail: Claude researches the term and reports that 'substitution motivation' is not an established term in the sport-volunteering literature, but grounds the idea in leisure-substitutability theory (Iso-Ahola) and offers to pull a short annotated set of bridging sources.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about substitution motivation and agree to receive a bridging annotated bibliography
nodes.detail: Says 'Sure' to Claude's offer to pull the Iso-Ahola piece and adjacent sources into a short annotated set.

nodes.label: Compile an annotated bibliography bridging substitutability and athletic-identity theory to the volunteer literature
nodes.detail: Runs further web searches and produces an annotated set covering Iso-Ahola (1986), Hendee & Burdge's substitutability literature, Bang & Chelladurai/Bang & Ross's VMS-ISE 'Love of Sport' factor, and athletic-identity/retirement-transition (continuity theory) literature, explaining how they fit together.

nodes.label: Prefer not to go too far and redirect back to the existing instrument and possible research questions
nodes.detail: Puts the literature bridging discussion 'in the parking lot' and asks to return to laying out research questions based on the existing instrument.

nodes.label: Compile a full slate of research questions mapped to the instrument, with a suggested execution priority
nodes.detail: Establishes a naming convention for the instrument's item tables, then lists eight research questions (RQ1-RQ8, including a construct-validity check and a qualitative mixed-methods question) each tied to specific variables and an analysis method, plus a suggested priority order for the results section.

nodes.label: Review the compiled research-question slate
nodes.detail: Reads through the prioritized eight-question slate before deciding how to proceed with the analysis.

Step 3.step_name: Data analysis plan for quantitative instrument
Step 3.step_action: Put instrument into Claude and ask for a data analysis plan based on research questions, instrument questions, and nature of data

nodes.label: Agree to follow Claude's suggestion that it will do analysis for the participant and ask whether exporting the real collected data would help refine the analysis plan
nodes.detail: Asks whether it would be better to refine the data-analysis plan using an export of the participant's actual collected data, and when Claude would like it.

nodes.label: Confirm the data export would help and specify what to verify
nodes.detail: Says to send the real data now, listing what it will check once it arrives (real sample/cell sizes, whether the substitution items behave as a coherent scale, variable coding/missingness, which research questions are actually answerable) and requests a CSV/Excel export.

nodes.label: Export and upload the fielded survey's response data from Qualtrics to Claude
nodes.detail: Exports the real Qualtrics response data as a zip file and uploads it to the chat.
nodes.softwares: Qualtrics, local file explorer, Chrome, Claude

nodes.label: Discover that the fielded instrument diverges from the drafted instrument and deliver a revised, data-grounded analysis plan
nodes.detail: Unzips and profiles the export (127 responses, missingness patterns), finds the drafted 5-item substitution scale isn't in the fielded survey at all (Q12 was restructured instead), computes item-pair correlations to check what actually functions as a substitution measure, identifies a usable Q4xQ7 comparison grouping, and revises the analysis plan to match what the real data can support -- then asks whether to run the full plan or revisit the research questions first.

nodes.label: Review the revised, data-grounded analysis plan
nodes.detail: Reads through the revised plan and instrument-discrepancy findings, also browsing Qualtrics' own Results dashboard (bar charts for Q3-Q13) directly before returning to Claude, before deciding how to proceed.

nodes.label: Examine questions and answers in Qualtrics and compare them with Claude's findings
nodes.detail: The participant examines the questions and answers in Qualtrics and compares them with Claude's findings about the fielded instrument.

Step 4.step_name: Test/refine data analysis plan with preliminary results collected so far in Qualtrics
Step 4.step_action: Give Claude exported results from Qualtrics survey and ask for data analysis plan refinement based on result formats

nodes.label: Ask to log the substitution-scale discrepancy as a reminder for later
nodes.detail: Asks Claude to put a pin in the substitution-scale discrepancy and remind the participant to check it against the instrument versus the Word version later.

nodes.label: Confirm the substitution-scale discrepancy is logged as a pinned reminder
nodes.detail: Records a pinned note describing the discrepancy between the Word-doc scale and the fielded instrument, to be revisited later.

nodes.label: Ask to continue the analysis plan and whether the data could support two papers
nodes.detail: Asks to keep going with the data analysis plan, starting slow, and whether the dataset could be split into two independent papers.

nodes.label: Propose and recommend a two-paper split structure
nodes.detail: Lays out a recommended split (general motivation paper vs. substitution paper) with two candidate paper framings -- 'Race Volunteer Motivation and Future Intentions' and 'Volunteering as Substitution for Race Participation' -- each mapped to specific research questions, plus an alternative quantitative-vs-mixed-methods split.

nodes.label: Review Claude's answer and then request a simple, runnable analysis plan for each paper
nodes.detail: Asks Claude to create a data analysis plan for each paper, kept simple enough to understand.

nodes.label: Build a step-by-step analysis plan table for each paper
nodes.detail: Produces a plain-language, numbered analysis plan (7 steps per paper covering cleaning, reliability, description, comparisons, and prediction/qualitative corroboration), flagging that the substitution measure is a single item rather than a validated multi-item scale.

nodes.label: Respond to Claude's question by mentioning qualitative Zoom interview data and ask about incorporating it into Paper 2
nodes.detail: Mentions having qualitative interview data in the form of Zoom transcripts and suggests pinning that for Paper 2 or revisiting after Paper 1 is outlined.

nodes.label: Log the Zoom transcripts as a pinned item and ask to begin running Paper 1's analysis
nodes.detail: Pins the Zoom transcripts for Paper 2's qualitative step, recaps the running pin list, and asks whether to start running Paper 1's cleaning and reliability steps on the real data.

nodes.label: Confirm starting Paper 1's data analysis and ask what analysis Claude can do as they are curious to explore possible analyses
nodes.detail: Agrees to start looking at data for Paper 1 and asks what kinds of data analysis Claude is capable of running.

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: use claude's plan to run paper 1 analysis

nodes.label: List the available statistical analysis capabilities
nodes.detail: Describes the descriptive, reliability, group-comparison, and regression analyses it can run directly on the dataset, and what it can't do (SPSS/AMOS-specific procedures like CFA with fit indices).

nodes.label: Examine Claude's suggestion of analyses and confirm running the reliability analysis, noting the participant can run further tests themselves in SPSS
nodes.detail: Agrees to run the recoding and reliability steps now, noting the participant can run other tests in SPSS if Claude tells them what to run and why.

nodes.label: Execute the reliability analysis on the real survey data
nodes.detail: Runs Cronbach's-alpha reliability checks across the candidate motivation subscales, reports every subscale clears an acceptable threshold, and flags a judgment call about combining vs. separating the sport-passion and sport-devotion items.

nodes.label: Check the Q11 and Q12 data in Qualtrics while Claude runs the reliability analysis
nodes.detail: While Claude runs the reliability analysis, the participant checks the Q11 and Q12 'People volunteer for races for different reasons' items in Qualtrics.

nodes.label: Review Claude's answer about combining and separating the scale, and decide to keep the sport-passion and sport-devotion subscales separate
nodes.detail: Explains there's a meaningful conceptual difference between wanting to be around the event and wanting to actively help others, so the two subscales should stay separate.

user_response.label: reject
user_response.reasoning: didn;t abopt the combine proposal of claude

nodes.label: Lock in the subscale structure and run the sample description and motivation-ranking analysis
nodes.detail: Confirms eight final subscales and runs the sample-description and motivation-ranking analysis, reporting altruistic/purposive motivation as the top-ranked motive and material incentives as the lowest.

nodes.label: Review Claude's answer and ask whether the subscales are framed in VMS-ISE's own terms
nodes.detail: Notes the participant used the VMS-ISE instrument and asks whether Claude's subscale labels match VMS-ISE's actual factor names.

nodes.label: Map the subscales to VMS-ISE's published factor structure and flag correspondence problems
nodes.detail: Maps the participant's ad hoc subscale labels to VMS-ISE's seven published factors, and flags two problems: 'Love of Sport' was split into two subscales, and 'Wellness' has no VMS-ISE equivalent, cautioning that this should be verified against the real item wording before writing it into the methods section.

nodes.label: Briefly check Claude's answer on VMS-ISE
nodes.detail: The participant briefly reads Claude's mapping of the subscales to VMS-ISE factors.

nodes.label: Pause to check personal notes on the instrument's original design rationale
nodes.detail: Opens a separate 'Instrument and Data Analysis Notes' document to recall why the instrument was originally structured the way it was.

nodes.label: Wait and pose a clarifying question about the scale adaptation
nodes.detail: Tells the participant to take their time and asks whether the participant set out to use VMS-ISE's full validated structure as-is or deliberately adapted/expanded it.

nodes.label: Recall that the instrument was a modified Bang & Chelladurai scale and ask about the love-of-sport factor
nodes.detail: Explains the Q11/Q12 blocks were a modified version of Bang & Chelladurai's VMS-ISE and asks whether Bang & Ross added a 'love of sport' factor found to be a strong motivator.

nodes.label: Confirm the Bang & Ross findings and explain how the instrument modified/expanded the original scale
nodes.detail: Confirms the Love of Sport factor's origin and validation history, and explains that the participant's instrument elaborates that single factor into more granular content (Sport Passion vs. Sport Devotion) plus a new Wellness dimension not in the original scale.

nodes.label: Agree to pull the actual VMS-ISE item wording for a precise comparison after reviewing Claude's explanation
nodes.detail: Agrees to let Claude search for the real Love of Sport item wording to check exactly which items map onto it.

nodes.label: Search for and verify the fielded scale's provenance against the actual published item wording
nodes.detail: Runs web searches and fetches the Bang & Ross (2009) source, builds a real item-by-item comparison table, concludes the instrument is an 'adapted and extended VMS-ISE' (Personal Growth dropped, Wellness and the substitution item newly added), and drafts methods-section language documenting the adaptation.

nodes.label: Frame the wellness items as an expression of health/active-lifestyle identity with a public-health angle by quickly reviewing the participant's old notes
nodes.detail: Explains the participant was purposefully looking at race volunteers' interest in healthy lifestyles and suggests it could be a public-health implication worth developing.

nodes.label: Elevate the Wellness subscale to a focal construct with a public-health framing
nodes.detail: Reframes Wellness as a focal construct rather than one of eight motivations, outlines ways to develop the public-health angle (within Paper 1, as a possible third paper, or via a link to self-rated health/activity level), and updates the pin list.

nodes.label: Review Claude's answer and confirm interest in the wellness/self-rated-health relationship
nodes.detail: Confirms the participant wants to explore whether Wellness motivation relates to self-rated health and activity level.

nodes.label: Run gender/age group comparisons and test the wellness/health relationship
nodes.detail: Runs gender t-tests and age ANOVAs across all subscales, then tests Wellness against self-rated health, activity level, and runner identity, reporting a positive-but-non-significant trend and explaining what that honestly does and doesn't support for the wellness-identity angle.

nodes.label: Confirm continuing to the next analysis steps after reviewing Claude's answer
nodes.detail: Says 'Yes' to continuing into the volunteer-type comparison and regression steps.

nodes.label: Run volunteer-type comparisons and the regression predicting future intentions
nodes.detail: Reports that only altruistic/purposive motivation differs significantly by volunteer type, and that a regression on future intentions shows Sport Devotion/Giving Back as the strongest predictor of intent to race again while Wellness trends negatively -- flagging this as a notable, counterintuitive finding for the wellness angle -- then notes all 7 planned steps for Paper 1 are complete.

nodes.label: Review the group-comparison and regression results
nodes.detail: Reads through the significant and non-significant findings -- including the negative wellness/future-intent relationship and the strong sport-devotion predictor -- before deciding what to do next.

Step 5.step_name: Create initial results with exploratory data analysis
Step 5.step_action: Analyze data with whatever capabilities Claude has without actually using statistical analysis software. Get an idea of initial findings.

nodes.label: Request a drafted methods-and-results section based on the completed analysis
nodes.detail: Asks Claude to draft an actual methods-and-results section from the completed Paper 1 analysis, rather than just a summary.

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: put analysis into draft as claude suggest

nodes.label: Draft a methods-and-results Word document for Paper 1, catching and correcting a coefficient-labeling error
nodes.detail: Builds an eight-page draft document covering participants, instrumentation (documenting the 'adapted and extended VMS-ISE' framing), procedure, and results tables; mid-draft, catches that it had mislabeled unstandardized coefficients as standardized (beta), recomputes the true standardized betas, and corrects the regression table before sharing the file.

nodes.label: Ask to use unstandardized B coefficients instead
nodes.detail: Reviews the draft and asks Claude to report unstandardized B coefficients instead of standardized betas.

nodes.label: Revert the regression table to correctly labeled unstandardized B coefficients
nodes.detail: Switches the regression table and surrounding text back to unstandardized B coefficients, re-renders the document to verify formatting, and re-shares the corrected file.

nodes.label: Note that this is just a draft and thank Claude while it revises
nodes.detail: While Claude revises the table, the participant types that it doesn't need to worry further since this is just a big-picture draft, and thanks it.

nodes.label: Confirm the file is saved and recap the open pins for next time
nodes.detail: Confirms the draft is saved and ready to pick back up, and reminds the participant of the three still-open pins (the substitution-scale discrepancy, the Zoom interview transcripts, and the wellness-identity angle) plus Paper 2's analysis.

nodes.label: Read Claude's final confirmation and wrap up the session
nodes.detail: Reads the closing recap of open pins and next steps before ending the recording.

Step 1.step_name: Analyze collected articles for research question support and framing
Step 1.step_action: Extract content from collected articles that support/frame research question rough drafts
Step 1.output: literature review-ready excerpts from articles that accurately reflect article findings and suggestions for further research
rubrics: substantive content extraction from existing articles that can be used to support research questions

ratings.output_quality_reason: Claude couldn’t do this, I couldn’t upload article pdf’s. I asked for workarounds, but they were very cumbersome and would have taken forever. I’ll have to think of a different method for this, or just do it manually.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: Claude couldn’t do this, I couldn’t upload article pdf’s. I asked for workarounds, but they were very cumbersome and would have taken forever. I’ll have to think of a different method for this, or just do it manually.

Step 2.step_name: Look at quantitative instrument and decide how to organize findings around research questions
Step 2.step_action: input instrument into Claude and ask for preliminary results outline
Step 2.output: preliminary results outline based on synthesis of research questions and instrument questions
rubrics: organizes potential results into direct research question/hypothesis answers

ratings.output_quality_reason: It took a few minutes for the AI to understand that the instrument was already created, but once I got it there, the output was pretty good.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: The output helped me to organize my thoughts/paper around some themes and research questions. I even asked it to split the output into 2 potential papers and it was able to do this.

Step 3.step_name: Data analysis plan for quantitative instrument
Step 3.step_action: Put instrument into Claude and ask for a data analysis plan based on research questions, instrument questions, and nature of data
Step 3.output: workable data analysis plan including statistical tests
rubrics: data analysis plan is clear and realistic
data analysis plan addresses all research questions

ratings.output_quality_reason: I feel like I’ll have to go back and check this output, since it directly impacts results and validity. I wouldn’t blindly trust a statistical analysis plan without checking. However, it seems like a very good starting point. It also brought up a few decision points that I felt I needed to be aware of, so that was a good exercise for me.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: It’s a good start, and helped me with some of the analysis questions. I feel more clear and confident about what questions I can answer with my data, and how.

Step 4.step_name: Test/refine data analysis plan with preliminary results collected so far in Qualtrics
Step 4.step_action: Give Claude exported results from Qualtrics survey and ask for data analysis plan refinement based on result formats
Step 4.output: refined data analysis plan based on actual results
Step 4.tools: Claude, Exported results file from Qualtrics
rubrics: data analysis plan is based on actual data formats
data analysis plan is detailed enough to actually execute

ratings.output_quality_reason: This was a good start, I feel like this reduced quite a bit of cognitive load and time for me. I will have to lay this out in a more organized way so that I can break it down further and make sure that I understand, but this was a great start that saved me alot of time.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: I feel like I have a good start, and I definitely got a good idea of what I’ll be working with when I’m ready to do data analysis. I even got a few preliminary results that were interesting to see the story of the data.

Step 5.step_name: Create initial results with exploratory data analysis
Step 5.step_action: Analyze data with whatever capabilities Claude has without actually using statistical analysis software. Get an idea of initial findings.
Step 5.output: Basic data analysis that indicates initial findings. Find out what claude can do with data analysis (!)
Step 5.tools: Claude, Results output file from either Qualtrics (or whatever claude needs to analyze)
rubrics: initial data analysis including descriptive data
If possible, any inferential data analysis that can be used to refine results or further data analysis

ratings.output_quality_reason: I was just curious to see what stories the results told. I’m presenting a rudimentary results summary later this year, and so I was basically curious if this would help me to formulate results for that. I was satisfied with a few of the outcomes, but I’m still curious of what else there is.
